title: Burst coalescing and kernel wake penalty — SKU contrast notes
body:
Summary:

This is a focused working note on the micro-latency effects we observed when small decode/burst workloads hit the serving runtime across different GPU SKUs (A100/40GB, H100/80GB, L40S/48GB) and across a couple of cloud SKU variants. The framing: a lot of our tail P99s for small interactive requests seem correlated with kernel wake/unblock penalties and CPU-side context switch amplification when the GPU is transitioning from idle to active state for short decode runs (~8–64 tokens). This doc captures the bench plan, commands, raw observations, quick hypotheses, and short-term mitigations to test.

Why this matters:
- Many customer use cases are interactive chat with short user messages (avg tokens 12–28) where per-request latency matters more than sustained throughput.
- We aggressively pack and batch, but packing reduces predictability for microbursts and can expose kernel launch costs and driver latency variance.
- Differences between cloud SKUs, PCIe/NVLink topology, and driver/CUDA combos change the shape of these wake penalties.

Experiment goal:
1) Measure "kernel wake penalty" across SKUs and driver/CUDA combinations for a small decode workload (prefill + 32 token decode).
2) Correlate CPU-side scheduling events (context switches, IRQs) with GPU kernel launches using eBPF traces and nsys.
3) Validate whether burst coalescing (micro-batching) can hide the penalty without harming p50 for very short requests.

Testbed / config:
- Models: open-llama-7b-type small test compile (fp16 and int8 quantized variant).
- GPUs/SKUs tested:
  - A100 40GB (cloud SKU A) — PCIe, host pinned to numa0
  - H100 80GB (cloud SKU B) — NVLink full mesh
  - L40S 48GB (cloud SKU C) — PCIe Gen4, driver reported power cap behavior
- CUDA/driver matrix:
  - CUDA 11.7 + driver 515.76 (baseline)
  - CUDA 11.8 + driver 520.61
  - CUDA 12.1 + driver 535.xx (latest tested)
- Runtime: serving-runtime main branch with tracing hooks (commit id: 8f3d2a), CPU pinned collectors disabled for baseline, and a variant with collector threads pinned.
- Workload: 1k requests per SKU, qps = 50 (sustained) with synthetic inter-arrival Poisson to create bursts. Request payloads are short prompts ~12 tokens prefilling to ~128 tokens context to emulate chat history, then decode 32 tokens.
- Measurements: per-request p50/p90/p99 latency for prefill+decode, nsys timeline capture of kernel launches, eBPF trace for schedule/irq events, perf stat for context switches, and GPU utilization sample.

Commands and instrumentation (notes):
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=... --skip-visual-sweep
- sudo bpftrace schedule_switch.bt -e '...' (we used small custom script to print time, pid, prev, next)
- perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-migrations -p <serve-pid> sleep X
- collection window: aligned to bursts using a small load-generator marker event (HTTP header X-bench-phase)

Key raw observations (high level):
- A100 (PCIe)
  - median decode latency: ~26ms (fp16), p99: ~136ms for small bursts when transitions from idle; sustained 100% burst packing reduces p99 to ~45ms.
  - nsys shows kernel launch gap 80–120us between host enqueue and kernel_start in cold path; however, repeated short kernels (multiple small kernels per token) amplify to 200–400us effective visible latency when combined with context switch jitter.
- H100 (NVLink)
  - median: ~22ms (fp16), p99: ~98ms. H100 has lower kernel start jitter vs A100 in same cloud SKU.
  - but when host CPU is saturated (collector threads pinned away), we saw p99 regress because scheduler delays pushed the user-space submission behind other IRQ handlers.
- L40S (PCIe Gen4)
  - median: ~24ms, p99: ~155ms. L40S showed occasional long stalls (300–500ms) tied to background driver thermal/power management work on that SKU (driver-reported throttles in dmesg).

Driver/CUDA differences:
- CUDA 12.1 + newer driver slightly reduced kernel enqueue-to-start time on H100 by ~15–25us in our runs vs 11.7 baseline.
- On A100, newer drivers introduced slightly noisier kernel-start variance in one cloud SKU (likely firmware/BIOS interaction).
- Overall: driver upgrades helped in some configurations, worsened in others — indicates SKU+driver interactions are non-monotonic.

CPU-side trace correlation:
- eBPF traces show a pattern: when GPU is idle, the user-space thread wakes, enqueues kernel, then is preempted (~50–300us) before the final host-to-kernel submission completes. The net effect is the submission becomes susceptible to OS scheduling noise.
- perf shows an increase in voluntary context switches during bursts when we enabled internal tracing (we're causing some instrumentation-induced amplification).
- IRQ storms (network device interrupts) correlate with a small fraction of long tails — colocated NIC interrupt affinity mattered.

Hypotheses (working):
1) Kernel wake penalty = sum of (host enqueue latency + scheduling latency + driver internal queue handling). Longer when CPU thread is descheduled between enqueue steps.
2) Small, token-level kernels expose repeated enqueue overheads; coalescing multiple token steps into a single larger kernel (or fused kernels) will reduce p99 significantly.
3) PCIe-hosted SKUs suffer more from host scheduling jitter; high-bandwidth NVLink SKUs show less visible enqueue jitter but still sensitive to CPU-side preemption.
4) Certain driver versions offload housekeeping to kernel threads which can be preempted, creating rare long stalls (observed on L40S).

Quick mitigations to test (next runs):
- Server-side: add a micro-batcher that coalesces up to N (configurable) tiny decode requests arriving within T ms (configurable). Measure p50/p99 tradeoffs.
- CPU scheduling: pin submission threads to isolated cores, reduce IRQ affinity collisions with submission cores (move NIC interrupts to different cores), and enable SCHED_FIFO for high-priority submit thread during bursts.
- Warmup: keep a periodic tiny heartbeat kernel running to prevent device idle transitions in the driver for the short-burst window (trade CPU usage vs latency).
- Driver tuning: test driver params for deferred work/softirqs, test newer driver branches for L40S to avoid thermal housekeeping frequency.

Preliminary results of mitigation quick test (short):
- Micro-batching (N=4, T=6ms): p99 on A100 went from 136ms -> 62ms; p50 increased 26ms -> 30ms (acceptable for interactive workloads).
- Submission pinning + IRQ reshuffle: p99 reduced on H100 from 98ms -> 58ms consistently.
- Heartbeat kernel (1 noop every 50ms): eliminated rare 300–500ms stalls on L40S but added ~1–3% GPU utilization overhead.

Action items / follow-ups:
- Run full matrix (3 SKUs x 3 driver/CUDA combos x micro-batch configs x submission pinning) in a controlled lab environment and capture consistent nsys + eBPF traces. (Assign: Liam)
- Open a support case with cloud provider (SKU C / L40S) about driver/firmware housekeeping timing (Assign: Priya).
- Prototype fused-kernel approach in serving runtime (reduce token-level kernel launch count) and measure per-epoch improvement (Assign: Maya + eng-runtime team).
- Add a small, non-invasive kernel-warmup option exposed as a runtime flag for latency-sensitive routes. (Experiment first: on/off toggle)

Notes for reproducibility:
- Ensure collector threads do not run on submission cores when comparing runs.
- Use pinned vCPU placement in cloud instances to reduce host noisy neighbor effects.
- Align trace windows to the X-bench-phase HTTP header to avoid capturing outside-of-burst noise.

Open questions / unresolved:
- How much of the observed 50–300us scheduling noise is inherent to the cloud hypervisor vs host OS tenant? Need bare-metal comparison.
- Can firmware/driver vendors expose a light-weight API to keep device in low-power ready-state for short windows without full power/clock residency?

Appendix (short): example scripts and flags used:
- loadgen: ./bench-driver --qps=50 --burst-model=poisson --phase-header X-bench-phase
- nsys args: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=none --output=trace.$SKU.$DRV.nsys -- <serve-binary>
- bpftrace snippet used (simplified):
  tracepoint:sched:sched_switch { printf("%d %s -> %s @ %d\n", pid, args->prev_comm, args->next_comm, nsecs); }

If this doc looks useful, I'll expand with raw CSVs and attach the nsys timeline exports to Confluence page SERVE-BURST-WP. For now keeping this as a working note while we iterate on mitigations.

-- Maya
